docs.title: SlicerSEEG
docs.text: Automated SEEG Electrode Localization for Epilepsy Surgery Planning

docs.title: From 4+ Hours to 30 Minutes
docs.text:
SlicerSEEG is a 3D Slicer extension that automates the localization of SEEG (Stereoelectroencephalography) electrodes from post-operative CT scans. Designed for epileptologists and neurosurgeons, this tool dramatically reduces manual processing time while maintaining clinical accuracy standards.

  • 90% Time Reduction

    Process cases in 15-30 minutes instead of 4+ hours of manual work

  • 98.8% Accuracy

    Sub-millimeter localization within 2mm clinical threshold

  • Deep Learning

    MONAI 3D U-Net for automated brain extraction

  • ML Confidence

    38-dimensional feature analysis with LightGBM

docs.title: Clinical Impact
docs.text:
Metric Performance Significance Localization Accuracy 98.8% within 2mm Gold standard clinical threshold Detection Sensitivity 100% No electrodes missed Processing Time 15-30 min 90% reduction vs. manual Precision 97.5% Minimal false positives Brain Segmentation Dice 0.936 Excellent structural agreement

Validated at Hospital del Mar

Clinical validation performed on 16-patient cohort at Hospital del Mar, Barcelona, Spain.

docs.title: Intelligent Trajectory Reconstruction
docs.text:
The enhanced trajectory reconstruction module goes beyond simple interpolation:

  • Semi-Automatic Mode: Uses detected contacts, fills gaps automatically
  • Manual Mode: User defines points, system estimates contacts
  • SEEG Convention: Proper labeling (deepest = 1)
  • Hemisphere Coloring: Blue (right) / Pink (left)

docs.title: Brain Extraction
docs.text: Automated brain segmentation using deep learning.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Brain extraction is the first step in the SlicerSEEG pipeline. It isolates brain tissue from the skull and other non-brain structures, which is essential for accurate electrode localization.

docs.title: MONAI 3D U-Net
docs.text:
SlicerSEEG uses the MONAI framework for brain segmentation:

  • Architecture: 3D U-Net with residual connections
  • Backend: PyTorch
  • Training Data: Medical imaging datasets

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: Metric Value Dice Coefficient 0.936 ± 0.011 Processing Time ~5 minutes GPU Acceleration Supported (CUDA)

docs.title: Input
docs.text:
• Pre-operative MRI (preferred) - Better soft tissue contrast
  • Post-operative CT (alternative) - If MRI unavailable

docs.title: Process
docs.text:
1. Preprocessing: Intensity normalization, resampling
  2. Inference: 3D U-Net predicts brain probability map
  3. Post-processing: Thresholding, morphological cleanup
  4. Output: Binary brain mask

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Brain_mask/
└── brain_mask_[timestamp].nrrd

docs.title: Automatic (Recommended)
docs.text:
When you click Apply in the main module, brain extraction runs automatically if:

  • An MRI volume is selected
  • No existing brain mask is provided

docs.title: Using Existing Mask
docs.text:
If you have a pre-computed brain mask:

  1. Load the mask volume into Slicer
  2. Select it in the MRI Input dropdown
  3. The system will use it directly (skips extraction)

docs.title: Preprocessing Steps
docs.text:
# Intensity normalization
normalized = (image - mean) / std

# Resampling to isotropic resolution
resampled = resample_to_spacing(image, [1.0, 1.0, 1.0])

docs.title: Post-processing
docs.text:
1. Thresholding: Probability > 0.5 → brain
  2. Largest component: Keep only largest connected region
  3. Hole filling: Fill internal cavities
  4. Morphological closing: Smooth boundaries

docs.title: Poor Segmentation Quality
docs.text:
Common Issues

  • Motion artifacts: Rescan if possible
  • Low resolution: Use higher resolution input
  • Wrong modality: MRI works better than CT

docs.title: Memory Issues
docs.text:
For large volumes:

# Reduce resolution temporarily
import SimpleITK as sitk
resampled = sitk.Resample(image, [128, 128, 128])

docs.title: Confidence Analysis
docs.text: ML-based electrode validation with 38-dimensional features.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: After centroid detection, each electrode candidate is evaluated using a machine learning classifier. This produces a confidence score (0-1) indicating how likely the candidate is a true electrode contact.

docs.title: 38-Dimensional Feature Vector
docs.text:
Each electrode candidate is characterized by features across four categories:

Spatial FeaturesIntensity FeaturesTopological FeaturesGeometric Features Feature Description RAS_X Right-Left coordinate RAS_Y Anterior-Posterior coordinate RAS_Z Superior-Inferior coordinate hemisphere Left (-1) or Right (+1) rel_position_X/Y/Z Normalized position in brain distance_to_center Distance from brain centroid Feature Description CT_mean Mean intensity at location CT_std Standard deviation CT_min Minimum value CT_max Maximum value CT_p25/p50/p75/p95 Percentile values intensity_ratio Relative to background Feature Description PCA_component_1/2/3 Principal component scores KDE_density Kernel density estimate neighbor_dist_mean Mean distance to neighbors neighbor_dist_min Distance to nearest neighbor louvain_community Community cluster ID n_neighbors_5mm Count within 5mm radius Feature Description distance_to_surface Distance to brain surface pixel_count Size of detected region aspect_ratio Shape elongation compactness Shape regularity

docs.title: LightGBM Classifier
docs.text:
SlicerSEEG uses LightGBM for confidence prediction:

  • Type: Gradient Boosting Decision Tree
  • Training: Patient-specific ensemble
  • Validation: Leave-one-out cross-validation

docs.title: Patient-Specific Ensemble
docs.text:
To avoid overfitting to specific patient anatomy:

# Leave-one-out prediction
for patient in cohort:
    # Train on all other patients
    train_data = cohort.exclude(patient)
    model = lightgbm.train(train_data)

    # Predict on held-out patient
    predictions[patient] = model.predict(patient.features)

docs.title: Score Interpretation
docs.text: Score Range Interpretation 0.8 - 1.0 High confidence (likely true electrode) 0.5 - 0.8 Medium confidence (review recommended) 0.2 - 0.5 Low confidence (possible false positive) 0.0 - 0.2 Very low (likely artifact)

docs.title: Threshold Selection
docs.text:
The Confidence Viewer allows real-time threshold adjustment:

Higher Threshold (e.g., 0.5)
├── Fewer candidates shown
├── Higher precision (fewer false positives)
└── May miss some true electrodes

Lower Threshold (e.g., 0.05)
├── More candidates shown
├── Higher recall (fewer false negatives)
└── More false positives to review

Recommended Starting Point

Start with threshold = 0.05 and adjust based on visual inspection.

docs.title: Output Files
docs.text:
Confidence_Analysis/
├── target_features_[timestamp].csv      # 38-dim feature vectors
├── confidence_predictions_[timestamp].csv # Predicted scores
└── confidence_summary_[timestamp].txt    # Statistics

docs.title: Feature CSV Format
docs.text: Column Description point_id Unique identifier RAS_X, RAS_Y, RAS_Z Coordinates feature_1...feature_38 Feature values confidence Predicted score prediction Binary (above threshold)

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Slider Control: Adjust threshold in real-time
  • Statistics Display: TP, FP, detection count
  • 3D Visualization: Color-coded by confidence
  • Export: Save filtered coordinates

docs.title: Using the Viewer
docs.text:
1. After processing, the Confidence Viewer panel activates
  2. Move the slider to adjust threshold
  3. Observe changes in 3D view and statistics
  4. When satisfied, proceed to trajectory reconstruction

docs.title: Performance Metrics
docs.text:
From clinical validation:

Metric Value Precision 97.5% ± 2.2% Recall 68.6% ± 13.6% F1 Score 0.797 ± 0.098 Mean Distance 0.91 ± 0.18 mm

Design Philosophy

The model prioritizes precision over recall. It's safer to miss contacts (which can be added manually) than to include false positives (which could mislead surgical planning).

docs.title: Feature Importance
docs.text:
Top contributing features (typical):

  1. CT_mean - Electrode metal is high intensity
  2. distance_to_surface - Electrodes penetrate brain
  3. neighbor_dist_mean - Contacts are regularly spaced
  4. PCA_component_1 - Linear arrangement
  5. louvain_community - Cluster coherence

docs.title: Image Enhancement
docs.text: Seven parallel methods for robust electrode detection.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
SEEG electrodes appear as high-intensity linear structures in CT scans. However, detecting them reliably requires multiple enhancement approaches to handle varying image quality and artifacts.

SlicerSEEG applies 7 parallel enhancement methods, generating 38 segmentation variants that are combined through ensemble voting.

docs.title: 1. CTP Enhancement (Frangi Filter)
docs.text:
Enhances tubular structures using the Frangi vesselness filter.

# Frangi vesselness filter parameters
frangi_enhanced = frangi(
    image,
    sigmas=range(1, 5),
    alpha=0.5,
    beta=0.5,
    gamma=15
)

Best for: Linear electrode shafts

docs.title: 2. Wavelet Denoising
docs.text:
Multi-scale denoising using PyWavelets.

import pywt

# Wavelet decomposition
coeffs = pywt.wavedec3(image, 'db4', level=3)

# Threshold detail coefficients
# Reconstruct denoised image

Best for: Noisy CT scans

docs.title: 3. Adaptive Thresholding
docs.text:
ML-predicted optimal threshold using Random Forest regression.

Input Feature Purpose Image histogram Intensity distribution Mean/std intensity Global statistics Edge density Structure complexity

Best for: Variable image quality

docs.title: 4. Morphological Operations
docs.text:
Shape-based refinement using mathematical morphology.

from scipy.ndimage import binary_opening, binary_closing

# Opening removes small bright spots
opened = binary_opening(mask, structure=sphere(2))

# Closing fills small holes
closed = binary_closing(opened, structure=sphere(2))

Best for: Cleaning segmentation artifacts

docs.title: 5. Histogram Enhancement
docs.text:
Statistical intensity normalization.

# Percentile-based windowing
p1, p99 = np.percentile(image, [1, 99])
enhanced = np.clip(image, p1, p99)
enhanced = (enhanced - p1) / (p99 - p1)

Best for: Inconsistent CT windowing

docs.title: 6. Percentile Thresholding
docs.text:
Distribution-based adaptive thresholds.

Percentile Typical Use 95th Conservative (fewer FP) 99th Standard 99.5th Aggressive (more detections)

Best for: Robust outlier handling

docs.title: 7. Gaussian Filtering
docs.text:
Multi-scale smoothing for noise reduction.

from scipy.ndimage import gaussian_filter

# Multi-scale Gaussian pyramid
scales = [0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0]
smoothed = [gaussian_filter(image, sigma=s) for s in scales]

Best for: High-frequency noise

docs.title: Why 38 Variants?
docs.text:
Each enhancement method generates multiple outputs with different parameters:

Method Variants Total CTP Enhancement 6 6 Wavelet 4 4 Adaptive Threshold 5 5 Morphological 4 4 Histogram 5 5 Percentile 6 6 Gaussian 8 8 Total 38

docs.title: Consensus Voting
docs.text:
# Global vote map
vote_map = np.zeros_like(image)

for variant in enhanced_masks:
    vote_map += variant

# Consensus at different thresholds
consensus_50pct = vote_map >= (38 * 0.5)  # 19+ votes
top_mask_1 = vote_map >= (38 * 0.8)       # 31+ votes

docs.title: Trajectory Reconstruction
docs.text: Enhanced semi-automatic electrode contact localization.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Trajectory Reconstruction module goes beyond simple linear interpolation to provide intelligent contact localization. It combines user-defined trajectory endpoints with detected electrode contacts, automatically filling gaps and following SEEG labeling conventions.

docs.title: Semi-Automatic Mode
docs.text:
Best for: High-quality CT scans with good electrode visibility

Step Action 1 User defines entry point (skull surface) 2 User defines deepest point (brain target) 3 System finds detected contacts along trajectory 4 System fills missing contacts automatically 5 Output: Complete contact sequence 
# Semi-automatic workflow
detected_contacts = electrode_predictions.get_points()
nearby = find_contacts_near_trajectory(detected_contacts, entry, deepest)
filled = fill_missing_contacts(nearby, spacing=3.5)

docs.title: Manual Mode
docs.text:
Best for: Challenging cases or verification

Step Action 1 User defines entry point 2 User defines deepest point 3 System estimates contact count from length 4 System generates equally-spaced contacts 
# Manual workflow
n_contacts = estimate_contact_count(entry, deepest, spacing=3.5)
contacts = linear_interpolate_contacts(entry, deepest, n_contacts)

docs.title: Smart Contact Detection
docs.text:
Finds detected contacts within configurable distance threshold of the trajectory line:

def find_contacts_near_trajectory(detected, entry, deepest, threshold=3.5):
    """
    For each detected contact:
    1. Calculate perpendicular distance to trajectory line
    2. If distance < threshold: include contact
    3. Sort by position along trajectory
    """

Parameters:

  • distance_threshold: Maximum perpendicular distance (default: 3.5mm)
  • Contacts beyond endpoints (±10% margin) are included

docs.title: Automatic Gap Filling
docs.text:
When contacts are missed by detection, the system estimates their positions:

def fill_missing_contacts(detected, entry, deepest, spacing=3.5):
    """
    1. Generate expected positions based on spacing
    2. For each expected position:
       - If detected contact within tolerance: use detected
       - Otherwise: use interpolated position
    """

Example: 

Expected:  1    2    3    4    5    6    7    8
Detected:  *         *    *         *         *
Filled:    D    I    D    D    I    D    I    D

D = Detected contact used
I = Interpolated (gap filled)

docs.title: SEEG Convention Labeling
docs.text:
Contacts are labeled following standard SEEG convention:

  • Deepest contact = 1 (closest to target structure)
  • Numbers increment toward entry point
  • Format: {electrode_name}{contact_number}

Example: Electrode "A" with 10 contacts 

A1  (deepest, in target)
A2
A3
...
A10 (most superficial, near entry)

docs.title: Spline Interpolation
docs.text:
For curved trajectories, cubic spline fitting is available:

from scipy.interpolate import splprep, splev

# Fit spline through control points
tck, u = splprep([x, y, z], s=0, k=3)

# Evaluate smooth curve
smooth_points = splev(np.linspace(0, 1, 50), tck)

When to Use Spline

Most SEEG electrodes are straight. Use spline only if visible curvature exists.

docs.title: Snap-to-Point
docs.text:
User clicks automatically snap to nearest detected point:

def snap_to_nearest_point(click, detected_points, max_distance=5.0):
    """
    If detected point within max_distance: snap to it
    Otherwise: use original click position
    """

docs.title: Markup Fiducials
docs.text:
Each contact appears as a labeled point:

  • Node name: Electrode_{name} (e.g., Electrode_A)
  • Point labels: A1, A2, A3...
  • Visualization: Colored spheres in 3D view

docs.title: Trajectory Curves
docs.text:
A line connects all contacts:

  • Node name: Trajectory_{name} (e.g., Trajectory_A)
  • Type: Linear curve through control points

docs.title: Hemisphere Color Coding
docs.text:
Colors indicate hemisphere based on R coordinate (RAS):

Hemisphere R Coordinate Color Right R ≥ 0 Blue (0.3, 0.5, 1.0) Left R < 0 Pink (1.0, 0.4, 0.7)

docs.title: 1. Select Mode
docs.text:
In the Manual Trajectory Definition panel:

  • [x] Semi-Automatic (uses Electrode_Predictions)
  • [ ] Manual

docs.title: 2. Enter Electrode Name
docs.text: Type the electrode identifier: A, B, C, etc.

docs.title: 3. Configure Spacing
docs.text:
Adjust contact spacing (default: 3.5mm)

Common values:

Electrode Type Typical Spacing Standard depth 3.5 mm High-density 2.0 mm Subdural 5.0-10.0 mm

docs.title: 4. Select Entry Point
docs.text:
1. Click "Select Entry Point"
  2. In 3D view, click on skull surface where electrode enters
  3. Point snaps to nearest detected contact if available

docs.title: 5. Select Deepest Point
docs.text:
1. Click "Select Deepest Point"
  2. In 3D view, click on deepest visible contact
  3. Point snaps to nearest detected contact if available

docs.title: 6. Reconstruct
docs.text:
Click "Reconstruct Trajectory"

Output: 

Console: Electrode A: R=-45.2 -> Left (Pink)
Console: Semi-auto trajectory: 8 detected, 4 estimated (filled)
Console: Created markup node: Electrode_A (12 contacts) - Left (Pink)

docs.title: 7. Repeat
docs.text: Process remaining electrodes (B, C, D, E, F, G...)

docs.title: Output Files
docs.text:
After saving the Slicer scene:

[patient_folder]/
├── Electrode_A.mrk.json      # Contact coordinates
├── Electrode_B.mrk.json
├── ...
├── Trajectory_A.mrk.json     # Curve nodes
├── Trajectory_B.mrk.json
└── ...

docs.title: Markup JSON Format
docs.text:
{
  "markups": [{
    "type": "Fiducial",
    "coordinateSystem": "LPS",
    "controlPoints": [
      {"label": "A1", "position": [-45.2, 12.3, -8.1]},
      {"label": "A2", "position": [-43.8, 11.9, -6.2]},
      ...
    ]
  }]
}

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
You can validate reconstructed trajectories against ground truth using the provided validation script:

python trajectory_validation.py

This calculates:

  • DSC: Dice similarity coefficient
  • Precision/Recall/F1: Detection metrics
  • Distance: Mean error to ground truth contacts

See Clinical Validation for validation methodology.

docs.title: Tips for Best Results
docs.text:
Point Selection

  • Zoom in for precise placement
  • Use orthogonal views (axial, sagittal, coronal)
  • Enable point snapping for consistency

Gap Filling

  • Keep "Fill Missing Contacts" enabled for complete trajectories
  • Review filled contacts visually for accuracy

Multiple Electrodes

  • Process electrodes systematically (A→B→C...)
  • Save scene periodically
  • Export each electrode after verification

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: This guide walks you through installing SlicerSEEG on your system.

docs.title: System Requirements
docs.text:
Component Minimum Recommended 3D Slicer 5.0+ 5.6.2+ RAM 8 GB 16 GB Storage 2 GB 5 GB GPU Optional CUDA-compatible

GPU Acceleration

A CUDA-compatible GPU can significantly speed up the deep learning brain extraction step, but is not required.

docs.title: Step 1: Install 3D Slicer
docs.text:
If you don't have 3D Slicer installed:

  1. Download from slicer.org
  2. Install following the platform-specific instructions
  3. Launch 3D Slicer

docs.title: Step 2: Install Python Dependencies
docs.text:
SlicerSEEG requires several Python packages. Open the Python Interactor in Slicer:

View → Python Interactor (or press Ctrl+3)

docs.title: Automatic Installation (Recommended)
docs.text:
Copy and paste this code:

import urllib.request
exec(urllib.request.urlopen(
    'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rociavl/SlicerSEEG/main/setup_dependencies.py'
).read().decode())

Installation Time

This process takes 2-5 minutes depending on your internet connection. You'll see progress messages in the console.

docs.title: Manual Installation (Alternative)
docs.text:
If the automatic installation fails, install packages manually:

import subprocess
import sys

packages = [
    'lightgbm',      # Confidence analysis
    'torch',         # Deep learning backend
    'monai',         # Medical imaging AI
    'networkx',      # Graph analysis
    'plotly',        # Interactive visualization
    'reportlab',     # PDF generation
    'pywavelets',    # Wavelet denoising
]

for pkg in packages:
    print(f"Installing {pkg}...")
    subprocess.check_call([sys.executable, '-m', 'pip', 'install', pkg])

print("Installation complete!")

docs.title: Option A: Manual Installation
docs.text:
1. Download the latest release from GitHub

  2. Extract the archive to a location of your choice

  3. Add module path in Slicer:

  4. Go to Edit → Application Settings → Modules
  5. Click the >> button under "Additional module paths"
  6. Navigate to the SEEG_ElectrodeLocalization folder

  7. Click Select Folder

  8. Restart 3D Slicer

docs.title: Option B: Clone from GitHub
docs.text:
For developers who want the latest version:

git clone https://github.com/rociavl/SlicerSEEG.git

Then add the path to Slicer as described above.

docs.title: Step 4: Verify Installation
docs.text:
After restarting Slicer:

  1. Open the Module Selector (dropdown in toolbar)
  2. Navigate to Segmentation → SEEG ElectrodeLocalization
  3. The module panel should appear

Installation Successful

If you see the module panel with input selectors and the "Apply" button, installation is complete!

docs.title: Module Not Found
docs.text:
If the module doesn't appear:

  1. Check that the path in Application Settings → Modules is correct
  2. Ensure you selected the SEEG_ElectrodeLocalization folder (not its parent)
  3. Restart Slicer completely

docs.title: Import Errors
docs.text:
If you see Python import errors:

# Check if packages are installed
import lightgbm
import torch
import monai
print("All packages imported successfully!")

If any import fails, reinstall that specific package.

docs.title: Memory Issues
docs.text:
For large CT scans (>512x512x512):

  • Close other applications
  • Increase Slicer's memory limit in Edit → Application Settings → General
  • Consider downsampling the input volume

docs.title: Dependencies Reference
docs.text:
Full list of required packages:

Package Version Purpose numpy ≥1.20.0, <2.0 Array operations scipy ≥1.7.0 Scientific computing pandas ≥1.3.0 Data manipulation SimpleITK ≥2.0.0 Medical image I/O scikit-image ≥0.18.0 Image processing scikit-learn ≥1.0.0 Machine learning lightgbm ≥3.3.0 Confidence analysis torch ≥1.10.0 Deep learning monai ≥0.9.0 Medical imaging AI networkx ≥2.6.0 Graph analysis matplotlib ≥3.4.0 Plotting plotly ≥5.0.0 Interactive viz pywavelets ≥1.1.0 Wavelet denoising reportlab ≥3.6.0 PDF generation

See requirements.txt for the complete list.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: Now that SlicerSEEG is installed, proceed to the Quick Start Guide to process your first case.

docs.title: Quick Start Guide
docs.text: Process your first SEEG case in 30 minutes.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The SlicerSEEG workflow consists of four main phases:

graph LR
    A[Load Data] --> B[Run Processing]
    B --> C[Review Results]
    C --> D[Reconstruct Trajectories]
    D --> E[Export]

docs.title: Required Input
docs.text: • Post-operative CT scan with implanted SEEG electrodes

docs.title: Optional Input
docs.text: • Pre-operative MRI for brain mask generation (improves accuracy)

docs.title: Loading Data
docs.text:
1. Drag and drop your DICOM/NRRD/NIFTI files into Slicer, or
  2. Use File → Add Data to import volumes

Naming Convention

Name your volumes descriptively (e.g., "PostOp_CT", "PreOp_MRI") for easier identification.

docs.title: Open the Module
docs.text:
1. Click the Module Selector in the toolbar
  2. Navigate to Segmentation → SEEG ElectrodeLocalization

docs.title: Configure Inputs
docs.text: Setting Selection MRI Input Pre-operative MRI (or existing brain mask) CT Input Post-operative CT with electrodes Output Folder (Optional) Custom name for results

docs.title: Run Processing
docs.text:
1. Click Apply
  2. Monitor progress in the Python console
  3. Wait 15-30 minutes for completion

Processing Time

  • Brain extraction: ~5 minutes
  • Image enhancement: ~10 minutes
  • Confidence analysis: ~5 minutes

docs.title: Using the Confidence Viewer
docs.text:
After processing completes, the Confidence Viewer panel activates:

  1. Threshold Slider: Adjust to filter electrode candidates
  2. Higher = fewer candidates, more confident

  3. Lower = more candidates, broader coverage

  4. Statistics Display: Shows detection metrics in real-time

  5. 3D Visualization: Electrodes appear as colored points

docs.title: Recommended Workflow
docs.text:
1. Start with default threshold (0.05)
  2. Visually inspect detected electrodes in 3D view
  3. Adjust threshold if needed:
  4. Too many false positives? → Increase threshold
  5. Missing electrodes? → Decrease threshold

docs.title: Phase 4: Reconstruct Trajectories
docs.text: The Manual Trajectory Definition section allows you to create complete electrode trajectories.

docs.title: Select Mode
docs.text: Mode When to Use Semi-Automatic Good electrode visibility, uses detected contacts Manual Challenging cases, full user control

docs.title: Create a Trajectory
docs.text:
1. Enter electrode name (A, B, C...)
  2. Click "Select Entry Point" → Click on skull surface in 3D view
  3. Click "Select Deepest Point" → Click on deepest contact
  4. Adjust spacing if needed (default: 3.5mm)
  5. Click "Reconstruct Trajectory"

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
• Markup points appear for each contact (A1, A2, A3...)
  • Trajectory line connects all contacts
  • Colors indicate hemisphere:
  • Blue = Right (R ≥ 0)
  • Pink = Left (R < 0)

docs.title: Repeat for All Electrodes
docs.text: Process each electrode (A, B, C, D, E, F, G...) following the same steps.

docs.title: Output Location
docs.text:
Results are saved to: 

~/Documents/SEEG_Results/[your_folder_name]/

docs.title: Output Files
docs.text: Folder Contents Brain_mask/ Deep learning brain segmentation Enhanced_masks/ 38 enhancement variants Global_masks/ Consensus masks (top_mask_1, top_mask_2) Confidence_Analysis/ Feature vectors, predictions, summary

docs.title: Exporting Coordinates
docs.text:
To export electrode coordinates:

  1. In 3D Slicer, select the Electrode_* markup nodes
  2. Right-click → Export to File
  3. Choose CSV or JSON format

docs.title: Image Quality
docs.text:
CT Scan Quality

  • Use high-resolution CT (0.5-1mm slice thickness)
  • Ensure electrodes are clearly visible
  • Avoid motion artifacts

docs.title: Processing
docs.text:
Memory Management

  • Close unnecessary applications
  • For large scans, consider cropping to brain region first

docs.title: Trajectory Reconstruction
docs.text:
Accurate Point Selection

  • Zoom in when selecting entry/deepest points
  • Use orthogonal views for precise placement
  • Enable "Fill Missing Contacts" for better coverage

docs.title: Example Workflow
docs.text:
1. Load PostOp_CT.nrrd
2. Load PreOp_MRI.nrrd (optional)
3. Open SEEG ElectrodeLocalization module
4. Select inputs, click Apply
5. Wait ~20 minutes
6. Adjust confidence threshold to 0.05
7. Create trajectory A: entry → deepest → Reconstruct
8. Create trajectory B: entry → deepest → Reconstruct
9. ... repeat for all electrodes ...
10. Export Electrode_A.mrk.json, Electrode_B.mrk.json, etc.
